read.sections.0.heading.back: Trade connects places in a network
read.sections.0.heading.source: Trade links places into a network

read.sections.0.text.back: Trade means giving goods to get other goods or money in return. Goods are things that people make or grow, such as tea, jars or cloth. In this made-up network, the hill village sends tea by ox cart to Riverstone. Boats carry the tea and clay jars made in Riverstone down the river to Coastport. At this port, traders exchange them for cloth and salt from ships that stop by. Not a single trader makes the whole journey. Each person carries the goods along part of the route. Together, these connections form a network. If the river water is too shallow for boats, traders have to find another way.
read.sections.0.text.source: Trade means giving goods to get other goods or money back. Goods are things people make or grow, like tea, jars or cloth. In the fictional network, the hill village sends tea by cart to Riverstone. Boats carry the tea and Riverstone's clay jars down the river to Coastport. At this port, traders swap them for cloth and salt from visiting ships. No single trader makes the whole journey. Each person carries the goods along one part of the route. Together, these links form a network. If the river is too low for boats, traders must find another way.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Trade means giving something to get something back. Goods are things that people make or grow. Ox carts carry tea from the hill village to Riverstone. Boats carry tea and jars to Coastport. At the port, people exchange them for cloth and salt. Not a single person makes the whole journey. Each person only travels part of the route. All these connections form a network. If the river is shallow, traders have to find a new way.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Trade means giving something to get something back. Goods are things people make or grow. A cart takes tea from the hill village to Riverstone. Boats take tea and jars to Coastport. At the port, people swap them for cloth and salt. No one person makes the whole trip. Each person does one part of the route. All the links make a network. If the river is low, traders need a new way.

read.sections.1.text.back: Real trade networks are much bigger. The Silk Road began more than 2,000 years ago. The Silk Road was many land and sea routes, not one road, and connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Silk from China was carried west, while horses and glass were carried east. In the Indian Ocean, sailors used the monsoon winds, which change direction twice a year. Ships could sail out with one wind and return with the next wind. Ports in East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia and China traded spices, cloth, gold and fine pottery. In Africa, camels crossed the Sahara Desert, carrying salt south and gold north. Timbuktu, in the Mali Empire, became rich from this trade.
read.sections.1.text.source: Real trade networks were much bigger. The Silk Roads began more than 2,000 years ago. They were many land and sea routes, not one road, and they linked China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Silk from China travelled west, while horses and glass travelled east. On the Indian Ocean, sailors used the monsoon winds, which change direction twice a year. Ships could sail out on one wind and come home on the next. Ports in East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia and China traded spices, cloth, gold and fine pottery. In Africa, camels crossed the Sahara Desert, carrying salt south and gold north. Timbuktu, in the Mali Empire, grew rich from this trade.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Real trade networks are much bigger. The Silk Road began more than 2,000 years ago. The Silk Road was many land and sea routes. These routes connected China with faraway places in the west. Silk was carried west, and horses were carried east. In the Indian Ocean, ships used winds that change twice a year. So ships could sail out and come back again. In Africa, camels crossed the Sahara Desert. Camels carried salt south and gold north. This trade made Timbuktu rich.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Real trade networks were much bigger. The Silk Roads began over 2,000 years ago. They were many land and sea routes. They linked China to lands far to the west. Silk went west, and horses went east. On the Indian Ocean, ships used winds that change twice a year. So ships could sail out and come back. In Africa, camels crossed the Sahara Desert. They took salt south and gold north. This trade made Timbuktu rich.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Trade moves ideas as well as goods
read.sections.2.heading.source: Trade moved ideas as well as goods

read.sections.2.text.note: Back-translation check: In a lesson about deserts, 'gurunya' (its teachers) could be misread as 'gurun' (desert). Consider 'guru-gurunya'. I made no change because the meaning matches the English.
read.sections.2.text.back: Traders carried ideas as well as goods. Paper was first made in China, and the way of making paper later spread along the route to Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Religions and languages also moved with traders. Timbuktu became famous for its books and its teachers. In Riverstone, the potter's note shows an idea moving, because a trader who stopped by shared a new way of decorating jars. But trade did not help everyone equally. Some traders became rich, while others lost out. On some routes, traders also bought and sold enslaved people, that is, people who were forced to work for other people.
read.sections.2.text.source: Traders carried ideas as well as goods. Paper was first made in China, and papermaking later spread along the routes to Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Religions and languages also travelled with traders. Timbuktu became famous for its books and teachers. In Riverstone, the potter's note shows an idea on the move, because a visiting trader shared a new way to decorate jars. But trade did not help everyone equally. Some traders grew rich, while others lost out. On some routes, traders also bought and sold enslaved people, who were forced to work for others.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: People in China made the first paper. Traders carried this idea to other places. Religions and languages also moved along the route. In Riverstone, a trader showed the potter a new way to make jars pretty. That is an idea moving. But trade did not help everyone. Some traders became rich. Others lost out. On some routes, traders bought and sold human beings. They were enslaved and not free.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: People in China made the first paper. Traders took this idea to other lands. Religions and languages moved along the routes too. In Riverstone, a trader shows the potter a new way to make jars pretty. That is an idea on the move. But trade did not help everyone. Some traders got rich. Others lost out. On some routes, traders bought and sold people. These people were enslaved and not free.

write.example.back: First, the jar was made by a potter in Riverstone. Then, boat traders carried it down the river to Coastport, together with tea from the hill village. These places are connected by the ox-cart road, the river and the sea. At the port, a trader exchanged the jar and the tea for cloth and salt. Ideas can move when a sailor sees the pattern on the jar and copies it in his/her place of origin. This shows that trade can move ideas as well as goods.
write.example.source: First, the jar is made by a potter in Riverstone. Next, a boat trader carries it down the river to Coastport, with tea from the hill village. The places are linked by a cart road, a river and the sea. At the port, a trader swaps the jar and the tea for cloth and salt. An idea could travel when a sailor sees the pattern on the jar and copies it at home. This shows that trade can move ideas as well as goods.

watch.summary.back: This animated video tells the story of the Silk Road. The video explains how, more than 2,000 years ago, trade began to grow between China and the lands to the west. The Silk Road was not one road. The Silk Road was a network of many routes that connected cities across Asia with the Middle East and Europe. Most traders did not go along the whole journey. They carried goods along part of the route, then handed them over to other traders. Silk, spices, horses and many other goods moved along these routes. Ideas also moved. Beliefs, languages, art and new ways of making things spread from one place to another. Some of these changes still influence the way people live today. The video calls the Silk Road an early 'world wide web', because this road connected so many people.
watch.summary.source: This animated video tells the story of the Silk Road. It explains how, more than 2,000 years ago, trade began to grow between China and lands to the west. The Silk Road was not one road. It was a network of many routes that linked towns across Asia to the Middle East and Europe. Most traders did not travel the whole way. They carried goods along one part, then passed them on to other traders. Silk, spices, horses and many other goods moved along the routes. Ideas moved too. Beliefs, languages, art and new ways of making things spread from place to place. Some of these changes still shape how people live today. The video calls the Silk Road an early 'world wide web', because it linked so many people.
